examples: The records from that time have been lost, so there is no way of knowing the truth now.
With this level of funding, there is no way we can compete with large corporations.
My ability cannot even be compared with his.
In this economy, a pay raise is out of the question.
The details are confidential, so outsiders cannot possibly know them.
fields.explain:
Mainly used in written language, essays and newspapers. In conversation, it is usually replaced by とても〜ない／どうにもならない.
Often accompanied by phrases that emphasize hopelessness:今となっては, この状況では, そもそも,元より.
The first clause usually presents the circumstances that make the action impossible; the second clause is ～るべくもない.
Not used for advice or commands; it is the speaker's objective judgment.

• Expresses impossibility: "cannot possibly…", "there is no way to…". The speaker judges that something cannot be done/achieved because of circumstances, information or ability.
• Often used with verbs of cognition/evaluation such as 知る・理解する・想像する・望む・期待する, or as 比べるべくもない when there is a large gap in a comparison.
• Formal, rational nuance; suited to written language and analytical writing. Close to "どうしようもない/不可能だ" but more objective and calm.
• It is a strong negation of feasibility, not simply "should not" (unlike ～べきではない).
fields.notes:
• "べく" comes from the continuative form of "べし" (possibility/worthiness); in this pattern it becomes a negation of feasibility, "～べくもない".
• Appears often in newspaper commentary, novels and academic texts.
• "想像するべくもない" is used, but "想像に難くない" is a different pattern meaning "it is not hard to imagine". Do not confuse them.
mistakes: Confusing it with ～べきではない (should not). Tip: ～べくもない = impossibility; ～べきではない = morality/advice.
Using it too much in natural spoken language sounds forced. In conversation, replace it with ～ようがない/無理だ.
The JLPT often sets traps with "AはBと比べるべくもない" vs "AはBに比べるべくもない". Using と or は～と… is natural; に is incorrect.
Commands/volition are not used after ～べくもない.

rows: Similar meaning but neutral and more conversational.
<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby><ruby>先<rt>さき</rt></ruby>がないので、<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らせようがない。
Negates possibility but leans toward emotion.
あの<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>が<ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けるわけがない。
Different axis of meaning: "should not" vs "cannot".
そんな<ruby>言<rt>いいかた</rt></ruby>い<ruby>方<rt></rt></ruby>はすべきではない。
Conversational; ～<ruby>比<rt>くら</rt></ruby>べるべくもない is written language.
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>才能<rt>さいのう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>とは<ruby>比<rt>くら</rt></ruby>べものにならない。

examples: Examinees shall carry their identification at all times.
Applications shall be submitted by email.
Entry after the starting time shall not be permitted.
Anyone who violates these rules shall be subject to disciplinary action.
Transportation costs shall be borne by the applicant.
fields.explain:
Used in regulations, contracts and official notices. Avoid it in everyday conversation.
Often used with regulatory nouns:本規程／本学／当社／当委員会／第○条など.
Combined with ただし、但し書き to state exceptions: ただし、緊急時はこの限りではない。
V-ない + ものとする can be used to prohibit/prevent an action.

• Normative language: "(we/the regulations) stipulate that…", equivalent to "shall" in legal English.
• The subject is usually omitted; those it applies to are "受験者／参加者／申請者／本学／本契約 など".
• Stiff, objective nuance; does not express personal volition at the time of speaking.
• Often appears in clauses of provisions: 条・項・但し書き etc.
fields.notes:
• The structure "ものとする" makes the text more normative and limits vague interpretation.
• In contracts, it often accompanies definitions: 用語の定義は別紙に定めるものとする。
• In softer announcements, companies often use ～こととする to sound friendlier.
mistakes: Using it in everyday conversation sounds stiff and funny.
Confusing it with ～とみなす: "regard as" ≠ "shall/is stipulated to".
Wrong agent: normative sentences usually do not state "I/we"; use the organization's name, or it is omitted.
The JLPT often sets traps with polite choices: for a strict regulation → choose ～るものとする, not ～ことにする (a personal decision).

rows: Softer; used in internal notices/formal conversation.
<ruby>来月<rt>らいげつ</rt></ruby>から<ruby>値上<rt>ねあ</rt></ruby>げすることとする。
Has several meanings; in legal texts often used as N + とする.
<ruby>提出<rt>ていしゅつ</rt></ruby><ruby>期限<rt>きげん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>金曜<rt>きんよう</rt></ruby>とする。
General in nature, no regulatory force.
<ruby>約束<rt>やくそく</rt></ruby>は<ruby>守<rt>まも</rt></ruby>るものだ。
<ruby>欠席<rt>けっせき</rt></ruby>は<ruby>辞退<rt>じたい</rt></ruby>とみなす。

examples: The moment the bell rang, the students rushed out of the classroom.
As soon as he opened the door, he apologized loudly.
The moment she arrived at the station, she made a phone call.
The moment she saw his face, his mother's eyes filled with tears.
As soon as the whistle blew to start the match, both teams went on the attack.
fields.explain:
The second clause is something that happens instantly (with no delay): ～た／～たのだ/～出した など.
Avoid commands/suggestions/the speaker's volition in the second clause.
Works well in literary descriptions or news to create a sense of urgency.
Often used with verbs of instantaneous action:立つ・出る・開く・鳴る・見る.

• Expresses two events in sequence that are almost simultaneous: "as soon as … then … immediately".
• Narrative, formal nuance; used a lot in written language, books and newspapers, and in describing sudden events.
• The subjects of the two clauses are usually the same person/thing; if they differ, this must be clear and natural in context.
• Not used to express repeated habits; it refers to a one-time, instantaneous event.
fields.notes:
• "否" is read いな; in everyday writing the whole phrase is often written in kana as "やいなや" for readability.
• Compared with ～とすぐ, ～や否や is more formal and dramatic.
• In news/incident reports, it helps create a fast pace and a narrative that emphasizes the point in time.
mistakes: Using a command/suggestion in the second clause is incorrect: ×着くや否や、連絡してください。
Using it for repeated habits is inappropriate. This pattern describes a one-time event.
Wrong tense: V-る is required before や否や; V-た is not used.
Exam questions often set traps with ～たとたん／～か～ないかのうちに: note the formal nuance and the strong "immediacy" of ～や否や.

rows: More conversational; the second clause is not the subject's volitional act.
<ruby>立<rt>た</rt></ruby>ち<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がったとたん、めまいがした。
Emphasizes overlapping time; used in both written language and conversation.
<ruby>授業<rt>じゅぎょう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わるか<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わらないかのうちに<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>て<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>った。
Written language; the subject is usually the same person; the second clause is often an unexpected action.
<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>るなり<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>てしまった。
Formal/literary; not used with commands/the speaker's volition.
<ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>くや<ruby>否<rt>いな</rt></ruby>や、<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>した。

examples: He doesn't listen when warned, doesn't meet deadlines, and has even caused the company losses.
He got so hooked on gambling that he ended up borrowing money.
I ignored my cold, and I ended up in the hospital.
He broke his promises again and again, and ended up being abandoned by his friends.
The wasteful spending went on until his savings were down to zero.
fields.explain:
Placed at the end of a passage/sentence to sum up a bad outcome.
The first clause lists accumulated actions/problems; they can be linked with ～し、～し、… or ～て、～て、…
Not used when the result is positive. If it is neutral/good, use ～結果／～末に.
In spoken language, まったく／本当に can be added to strengthen the critical nuance.

• Expresses a bad outcome after a series of problems: "to the point that…", "in the end…".
• Carries the speaker's criticism/negative dissatisfaction; not used for good results.
• Often accompanied by words such as ついには・とうとう・あげく・結局 to emphasize "in the end".
fields.notes:
• "始末" originally means "settling/outcome"; in this pattern it leans toward "a bad, blameworthy outcome".
• Often appears in commentary criticizing attitudes/awareness: 管理が杜撰で～という始末だ。
• Can take a contracted form before a noun/phrase: ～という始末 (drop だ when the sentence continues).
meaning: In the end, it came to this… (bad outcome: 始末だ)
mistakes: Using it for a good result is incorrect: ×努力した結果、合格する始末だ → use 合格した.
Exams often set traps with ～あげく／～末に: if a critical nuance condemning someone's attitude is needed → choose ～始末だ.
Form: V-る + 始末だ; V-た is not used directly before 始末だ.
Without a preceding chain of circumstances, the sentence sounds forced. There should be a listing before concluding with ～始末だ.

rows: Emphasizes a long process before a bad result; more neutral in terms of personal criticism.
Neutral; the result can be good or bad.
<ruby>議論<rt>ぎろん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>末<rt>すえ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>合意<rt>ごうい</rt></ruby>した。
<ruby>検査<rt>けんさ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>結果<rt>けっか</rt></ruby>、<ruby>異常<rt>いじょう</rt></ruby>なし。
Expressive; does not specifically describe an accumulated chain like ～<ruby>始末<rt>しまつ</rt></ruby>だ.
<ruby>大切<rt>たいせつ</rt></ruby>な<ruby>書類<rt>しょるい</rt></ruby>をなくしてしまった。

examples: He has a tendency to exaggerate things.
The Japanese media tend to stir up sensationalism.
This plan tends to make light of costs.
Experts tend to use too much difficult jargon.
I am aware that I tend to be more particular about procedures than results.
fields.explain:
Situations: reports, academic comments, mild criticism.
Nuance: formal and distant; avoid using it directly to the listener's face.
Tense: mainly the general present; the past is less common but can be used to talk about an earlier period.
It is rarely combined directly with the negative; to soften it, use an adverb of degree instead of a negative.

～る嫌いがある expresses "having a tendency/leaning toward (a bad habit)", with a mildly critical, formal nuance that leans toward written language.
• Often used for habits and repeated tendencies, with a moderately negative evaluation.
• The subject can be an individual, a group of people, an organization, a policy, a document, etc.
• Often accompanied by adverbs of degree such as やや・少々・いささか・多少 to soften it.
• Not used for praise/positive things; for neutral cases use 傾向がある.
fields.notes:
• "嫌い" here is a Sino-Japanese noun meaning "tendency/bias", not "dislike".
• When talking about yourself to remain polite and modest, this pattern is suitable in self-evaluations.
• Often combined with evaluative phrases: 形式に流れる嫌いがある／数字に偏る嫌いがある／結論を急ぐ嫌いがある.
mistakes: Confusing it with "Aが嫌いだ (dislike A)": completely different meaning and function.
Using it directly with an i-adjective is incorrect: you do not say 真面目な嫌いがある; change it to a verb or noun + の.
Using it to praise is unnatural: this pattern implies criticism; for praise use 傾向がある or another expression.
Using it in casual conversation sounds stiff; the JLPT favors written contexts/objective judgments.

rows: <ruby>言<rt>いいわけ</rt></ruby>い<ruby>訳<rt></rt></ruby>に<ruby>走<rt>はし</rt></ruby>る<ruby>嫌<rt>きら</rt></ruby>いがある
<ruby>消費<rt>しょうひ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>増<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>える<ruby>傾向<rt>けいこう</rt></ruby>がある
Describes repeated habits; closer to spoken language

examples: The only person who can be entrusted with this matter is him.
I can't think of anyone other than Yamada as the next captain.
There is no instructor other than Professor Tanaka who is so well versed in Japanese culture.
The best sushi in this town is here and nowhere else.
The final candidate can be none other than this plan.
fields.explain:
Formal; often used in speeches, nominations, advertising and expert judgments.
Suitable when you want to emphasize uniqueness/being the best; avoid using it carelessly so as not to exaggerate.
他に/ほかに can be added for emphasis; "～ない" is required for the meaning.

• Asserts uniqueness: "apart from N, there is no other option".
• Nuance of high evaluation/praise and absolute trust; used in formal statements and promotion.
• Often used with nouns referring to people, organizations, places, means, or the best/only option.
• The second clause is always negative: ～ない／いない／考えられない／見当たらない.
fields.notes:
• When praising a person/organization, this pattern creates strong credibility in CVs, PR and speeches.
• Not used for trivial obvious facts; use it when there are clear criteria for comparison.
• Accompanied by negative verbs rich in nuance: 見当たらない／思い当たらない／他に類を見ない.
mistakes: Dropping "ない" in the second clause → wrong meaning. A negative is always required.
Using it for ordinary things → does not fit the nuance of "unique/outstanding".
Confusing it with ～しかない: the JLPT tests the difference between "uniqueness as an evaluation" and "no other choice".

rows: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>をおいて<ruby>他<rt>た</rt></ruby>にない
Neutral, little nuance of high regard
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby><ruby>以外<rt>いがい</rt></ruby>にいない
<ruby>夏<rt>なつ</rt></ruby>はビールに<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>る

fields.meaning: Taking… as the point in time
examples: I will be resigning as of today.
We will inform you of the results by email.
With this, we will close the meeting.
This document shall serve in place of a warranty certificate.
Approach one's work with enthusiasm.
Even with all his effort, it was hard to achieve.
fields.explain:
Very formal; used a lot in administrative and business documents and speeches.
When used in the meaning "point in time", it often goes with announcements of closing/opening, appointments and endings.
Meaning "by means of": abstract nouns/designating nouns are preferred (書面、文書、メール、愛、誠意、熱意、誠心誠意).

• Means/method: "by/through/thanks to" in official documents, notices and contracts.
• Point in time when something takes effect: "as of/until", to declare a start/end.
• Standard/treatment: determines what is regarded as…
• Be careful to distinguish it from ～をもってしても (a different pattern with a strong concessive meaning).
fields.notes:
• The kanji 以て is also seen in archaic/symbolic writing: ～を以て（＝をもって）.
• "身をもって" is an idiom: 自ら体験して (experiencing it oneself).
• In ceremonies, "これをもちまして" is a very natural way to open/close a speech.
mistakes: Confusing ～をもって with ～によって in spoken sentences → sounds stiff or too bookish.
Using ～をもって when the subject is the speaker in ordinary conversation → unnatural; replace with ～で/～で.
Confusing it with ～をもってしても: the JLPT often sets traps where しても requires a negative sentence.

rows: <ruby>書面<rt>しょめん</rt></ruby>をもって<ruby>通知<rt>つうち</rt></ruby>
メールにより<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>
これをもちまして<ruby>閉会<rt>へいかい</rt></ruby>といたします
<ruby>全力<rt>ぜんりょく</rt></ruby>をもってしても<ruby>無理<rt>むり</rt></ruby>だ

examples: This service has built its infrastructure on the premise of high traffic.
We restructured the curriculum on the premise of small class sizes.
This schedule is premised on cooperation between the two companies.
The event will be held on the premise that masks are worn.
The database was designed on the premise of future expansion.
fields.explain:
Combined with nouns related to operating conditions:利用・需要・前提人数・連携・拡張性・予算・安全基準.
Often goes with concrete actions:設計する・見直す・構築する・実施する・運用する.
"Implementation/operation-oriented" nuance; natural in field reports.

• Sets a concrete practical/implementation premise and carries out actions/design/adjustments based on it.
• Practical nuance, closer to the field than ～を前提として (which is normative/documentary).
• Common in IT, operations, service design and implementation planning.
fields.notes:
• Use "当面/仮に/想定上" to emphasize that the premise is temporary: 当面Xを前提に運用する。
• In design, there is the pair "前提" vs "制約": 前提 (assumption) and 制約 (constraint) should be kept separate in descriptions.
• When the premise changes, an action should accompany it: 前提変更に伴い、設計を見直す。
mistakes: Confusing its nuance with ～を前提として: exam questions ask you to choose the form that fits the context (normative vs operational).
Putting a long clause directly into ～を前提にして makes it heavy; use という前提で.
Vague premise: a concrete noun is needed; avoid an N that is too general to be measured.

rows: <ruby>少<rt>しょう</rt></ruby><ruby>人数<rt>にんずう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>前提<rt>ぜんてい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>運営<rt>うんえい</rt></ruby>
<ruby>信頼<rt>しんらい</rt></ruby><ruby>継続<rt>けいぞく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>前提<rt>ぜんてい</rt></ruby>として
Not necessarily an "assumption taken as true".
<ruby>規格<rt>きかく</rt></ruby>に<ruby>基<rt>もと</rt></ruby>づいて<ruby>設計<rt>せっけい</rt></ruby>
<ruby>需要<rt>じゅよう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>増<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>えるという<ruby>前提<rt>ぜんてい</rt></ruby>で

examples: When he got a job, he left his hometown.
Since the accident, the company's safety standards have been tightened.
This road is the boundary: the east side is residential and the west side is commercial.
From 1997 on, the regulations changed greatly.
Since the great earthquake, awareness of disaster prevention has increased.
From this point on, the team kept winning.
fields.explain:
Nouns used as the dividing point:年/年度/時点/出来事(結婚・出産・事故・震災)/地物(川・道・山脈・県境).
Often goes with verbs of change/shift:変わる・転じる・一変する・分かれる・境する.
Objective, descriptive nuance; suitable for reports, history, geography and statistics.

• "Taking N as the dividing point/boundary": indicates a clear before–after division in time or in space.
• In time: an event/point in time marks a turning point or a change in tendency.
• In space: an object/road/border serves as the boundary dividing areas.
• Emotionally neutral; different from ～を機に (deliberately taking an opportunity) or ～を限りに (ending).
fields.notes:
• "境" originally means "boundary". The figurative time meaning is very common in statistics/sociology.
• To clearly emphasize "before–after", use a contrasting structure: N を境に、前は～、後は～。
• In geography/administration, it goes with the verbs 分ける/区切る/接する to describe boundaries.
mistakes: Confusing it with ～を機に: exams often set traps with the "intentional" nuance (機). ～を境に is an objective description of a result.
Using it with nouns that are not a concrete dividing point/boundary sounds forced: prefer clear events/points in time.
Placing the subject badly makes the sentence ambiguous: make clear what the "before–after change" applies to.

rows: <ruby>事故<rt>じこ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>境<rt>さかい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>変化<rt>へんか</rt></ruby>
Implies deliberately using the occasion to do something.
<ruby>結婚<rt>けっこん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>機<rt>き</rt></ruby>に<ruby>禁煙<rt>きんえん</rt></ruby>
Indicates a time from a past point until now, does not emphasize a "boundary of change".
<ruby>卒業<rt>そつぎょう</rt></ruby><ruby>以来<rt>いらい</rt></ruby><ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>っていない
Stop at the end of N
<ruby>今季<rt>こんき</rt></ruby>を<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>りに<ruby>引退<rt>いんたい</rt></ruby>
Used for a series of events that follow.
<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>皮切<rt>かわき</rt></ruby>りに<ruby>全国<rt>ぜんこく</rt></ruby><ruby>巡回<rt>じゅんかい</rt></ruby>
